paras: The attempted lynching at Crestline, Ohio, was a mob's attempt on the night of April 21, 1882, to hang the man who had just shot and killed the village marshal, David Snodgrass. Citizens beat the prisoner and, by wire accounts, took him from jail to hang him before desisting. He was removed to the jail at Bucyrus the same evening and in July was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to life in the penitentiary.

For several days a man with "no visible means of support" had been loitering in Crestline, and Marshal Snodgrass had been watching him. On the evening of Friday, April 21, the man entered a hardware store where the marshal was talking with Dr. Jenner and asked to see some cartridges. Snodgrass questioned him and asked whether he had a revolver, and the man said he had one at home.

When the marshal took hold of him, the man broke away and ran, and within a few rods turned and fired. His second shot struck Snodgrass near the heart, at about 7:30 p.m., and the marshal died minutes later in a nearby drug store. The Stark County Democrat said he fired three times, while the Somerset Press and the Ravenna Democratic Press said twice.

Townspeople who joined the chase captured the man, and the Somerset Press wrote that "it was with great difficulty that the infuriated citizens were kept from lynching the fellow." Several of them struck him over the head and "beat and bruised him up considerable" before he reached the lockup. According to the Crestline wire, he was then "at once taken by a mob to hang, but they desisted," and a lynching was expected before morning. Weekly news summaries said the citizens made "two attempts to lynch the murderer."

The prisoner was taken to Bucyrus that evening and lodged in jail, "for safe keeping" in the words of the Napoleon Democratic Northwest. He refused to give his name, and Columbus policemen later identified him as Thomas O'Hagan, "a professional burglar." Indicted as James Hogan, he went on trial at Bucyrus on July 18. A Bucyrus special reported that the jury found "John Smith, alias James Hogen" guilty of second-degree murder and that he was sentenced to the penitentiary for life. No report of arrests or charges against members of the mob appears in the coverage.

The story reached distant papers as a short wire item, headed "Murdered a Marshal" in the St. Paul Daily Globe, which ran the night's prediction that the prisoner "will be lynched." The Salt Lake Herald's version said a mob "was barely prevented from hanging a burglar," and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer reprinted the jail-mob account two days later. Further from the scene, the Ellsworth American in Maine garbled the town as "Centreville, Ono" and guessed that the prisoner was "probably lynched."

Ohio weeklies gave fuller accounts told from the marshal's side, calling the prisoner a "tramp" or an "unknown man" and noting that Snodgrass "leaves a family." They reported the crowd's fury and the beating without criticism, and some, like the Ravenna paper, did not mention the mob at all. No article identified the race of either man, and the July verdict circulated as a brief telegram in papers from Washington to St. Clairsville.

Accounts differ on where the mob acted. The wire filed that night said the prisoner was taken out of the jail by a mob that then desisted, while the Somerset Press, the fullest Ohio account, placed the attempt at his capture, before he was put in the lockup. The two versions may describe different moments of the same evening, which would fit the summaries' report of two attempts.

bases: After the killing of Marshal David Snodgrass, citizens tried to lynch the captured suspect, beat him, and by wire accounts took him from jail to hang him before desisting; he was later tried and sentenced to life (A1, A2, A11, A20).

A mob of citizens tried to hang the accused killer of the marshal but desisted or was prevented, so no one was killed by the mob (A2, A5, A11); he was tried at Bucyrus and sentenced to the penitentiary for life (A20).
Independent Ohio weeklies and the Crestline wire agree that a crowd tried to lynch the prisoner and was held off (A2, A11, A13), though they differ on whether he was taken out of jail (A1, A11).
